newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan output up, but markets jittery on outlook.
newsitem.headline: Japan output up, but markets jittery on outlook.

text.p: Japanese output data on Wednesday backed the government view that the economy is recovering, but markets remained unconvinced, with the yen crashing to a new four-year low against the dollar and stocks remaining volatile.

In announcing its latest output data, the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) said industrial output was on an "upward trend", dropping the qualifier "gradual" which it had used since February last year.
The small step forward is in line with the government's view that the economy is recovering gradually.
MITI forecast a rise in output of 3.0 percent in the January-March period against the previous quarter, following a 3.3 percent rise in the October-December quarter.
A ministry official said the improvement was based on expectations that production would continue at high levels and inventories keep improving.

MITI forecast that manufacturers' output would rise 5.4 percent in January but fall 2.9 percent in February. The official said the drop in the February forecast was largely due to the strong January figure.
But economists said the real focus was on the outlook for the next fiscal year starting on April 1, when the government plans to raise the consumption tax to five percent from three.

"The problem is more what happens after fiscal 96/97. After the sales tax rises in April, the April-June quarter will definitely be negative," said Michinori Nishimura, an economist at LTCB Research Institute.
Asked whether it expected the rise in production to continue beyond April, the MITI official declined to comment, saying its forecast covered only the period up to the end of February.

But financial markets shared Nishimura's bleak outlook, selling the yen on the belief that the Bank of Japan would be forced to stick to its policy of keeping the discount rate at rock-bottom levels for a while.
The yen plummetted to a fresh 47-month low of 122.75 to the dollar in Tokyo trade and traders said it could fall further.
Currency dealers said the fall of the yen against the dollar was based on the relative strength of the U.S. economy and the resulting gap between high U.S. interest rates and low rates in Japan.
The gap has lured Japanese investors to higher-yielding foreign assets, including dollar-denominated bonds.

Many market participants believe that uncertainty over the economic outlook beyond April will tie the hands of Japanese authorities on monetary policy, despite their bullish view on the present state of the economy.

Although Tokyo stock prices rebounded strongly on Wednesday as the yen's fall invited purchases in shares of multinational companies, the market's recent weakness has been fueled by pessimism about economic prospects in the upcoming fiscal year.
Tokyo bourse's key barometer, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares, jumped by 538.73 points, or 3.03 percent, to close at 18,335.30.
